name: proc-lens
summary: A Linux kernel module that keeps process snapshots stable while they're being read.
intro: A Linux kernel module that periodically collects process information and keeps a snapshot stable for each open file.
points: A delayed_work task collects process data. Reference counting and locking manage object lifetimes, while each open file retains its snapshot even when a newer one is published.

The repository documents QEMU checks for partial reads, seek, concurrent readers, process creation and exit, and 50 load/read/unload cycles. The test environment is Ubuntu Linux 6.8.0-147-generic on x86-64.

A stable snapshot does not mean every field was captured at the same instant: RSS and scheduler values can change during collection. KASAN, lockdep, and allocation-failure injection have not been tested.

name: Gshare in gem5
summary: Compared four indexing operations in a Gshare branch predictor using gem5.
intro: We compared XOR, OR, AND, and XNOR indexing in a Gshare predictor on gem5's RISC-V O3CPU.
points: We kept the prediction table and counter configuration fixed and ran graph workloads. We compared branch mispredictions per thousand instructions (MPKI) alongside instructions per cycle (IPC).
The results depended on the workload. Comparing MPKI and IPC together helped us see how changes in prediction behavior related to execution performance.
source_note: Based on our course report, which is not publicly available.

name: xv6-riscv labs
summary: Exercises in system calls, scheduling, copy-on-write, and threads using xv6-riscv.
intro: Operating systems coursework built on MIT xv6-riscv and the course starter code.
points: The assignments cover shell behavior, system calls, stride scheduling, copy-on-write, memory allocation, and threads. They helped me trace a request from user code into the kernel and follow how scheduling and memory policies affect execution.
The repository includes assignment code and run instructions. The documented checks use one CPU; multicore synchronization and scheduling fairness need separate verification.

name: Zynq board labs
summary: Board exercises covering interrupts, BRAM, display control, and Linux device drivers.
intro: Embedded systems coursework on a Zynq board, using the supplied IP, BSP, and examples.
points: I worked with button interrupts, LED patterns, BRAM, and a TFT-LCD. Interrupt handlers updated state, while the main loop handled output. Other exercises used memory-mapped I/O and a character device driver to connect user programs to the board.
A busy-wait in the output loop can affect responsiveness even when interrupts are handled correctly. Following the whole path from input to output made that distinction easier to see.
